learn.b: Version control is a tool that remembers every version of your project. Instead of files named final, final2 and really_final, you keep one folder and the tool stores each saved snapshot. You can look back or return to any of them.

A snapshot in Git is called a commit. Each commit has an ID, an author, a date and a message. All the commits plus your files live in a repository, or repo for short. Git keeps its data in a hidden folder called .git.

Git is the program that runs on your computer and tracks changes. GitHub is a website that hosts Git repositories online so you can back them up and work with other people. You can use Git without GitHub, but not GitHub without Git.
Git stamps your name and email on every commit, so tell it who you are once. The --global flag saves the setting for every repo on your computer.
learn.code:
git config --global user.name "Ana"
git config --global user.email "ana@example.com"
git --version

learn.b: Run git init inside a project folder to turn it into a repository. Git creates the hidden .git folder and starts watching. Run it only once per project.
learn.code:
mkdir game
cd game
git init

learn.b: git status tells you what is going on: which files are new (untracked), which changed, and which are ready to be committed. Run it often, it is your best friend.

Git saves in two steps. First git add puts changes in the staging area, like a box you pack. Then git commit seals the box as a snapshot. This lets you choose exactly which changes go into each commit.
learn.code:
git add index.html
git add .
git status

learn.b: git commit -m with a short message saves the staged changes. Write messages that say what you did, like Add login page. Without -m, Git opens a text editor.
learn.code: git commit -m "Add login page"

learn.b: git log lists commits from newest to oldest, with ID, author, date and message. Press q to leave the list. For a short view use git log --oneline, which shows one line per commit.
learn.code:
git log
git log --oneline

learn.b: git diff shows lines you changed but have not staged yet. Lines starting with a minus were removed and lines with a plus were added. It is a great way to review your work before committing.
Once you git add a file, git diff shows nothing for it. To see what is staged and about to be committed, use git diff --staged.
learn.code:
git diff
git add app.js
git diff --staged

learn.b: git show followed by a commit ID displays that commit's message and changes. IDs are long, but the first 7 characters are usually enough.
learn.code: git show a1b2c3d

learn.b: Some files should never be committed: passwords, huge downloads, build output, and folders like node_modules. A file named .gitignore lists patterns Git must ignore. Git will not show or add matching files.
Put one pattern per line. A name ignores that file, a star matches any text, a trailing slash means a folder, and a line starting with # is a comment.
learn.code:
# secrets
.env
*.log
node_modules/
build/

learn.b: The .gitignore file itself is a normal file, and you should commit it so everyone shares the same rules. Create it before you add other files, so unwanted files never enter history.
Ignoring only works for untracked files. If Git already tracks a file, adding it to .gitignore is not enough. Stop tracking it with git rm --cached, which keeps the file on disk.
learn.code:
git rm --cached secrets.txt
git commit -m "Stop tracking secrets"

qs.q: What is a .gitignore file for?

qs.q: Which pattern ignores every file ending in .log?
qs.why: The star matches any name before .log.

qs.why: You must also run git rm --cached.

learn.b: A branch is a separate line of work. You can try a new feature on its own branch without touching the main one. If it works you merge it in, and if not you just delete it. Branches are cheap and fast in Git.
git branch name makes a branch, and git switch name moves you onto it. The shortcut git switch -c name does both at once. git branch alone lists branches, with a star on the current one.
learn.code:
git branch
git switch -c login
git switch main

learn.b: HEAD is Git's pointer to where you are now, usually the tip of your current branch. When you commit, the current branch moves forward and HEAD goes with it. Older tutorials use git checkout in place of git switch.
After a branch is merged you can remove it with git branch -d name. Git refuses if the work is not merged yet, which protects you. A capital -D forces the delete.
learn.code: git branch -d login

learn.b: To bring a branch's work into another, switch to the receiving branch and run git merge with the other branch's name. For example, to put login into main, be on main and merge login. Git joins the histories with a new merge commit or by just moving forward.
learn.code:
git switch main
git merge login

learn.b: If main has no new commits since you branched, Git simply moves main forward to the branch tip. This is called a fast-forward and makes no extra merge commit. If both branches changed, Git creates a merge commit.
A conflict happens when two branches changed the same lines of the same file. Git cannot guess which is right, so it stops and asks you. git status lists the files with conflicts.
Open the file and look for markers: lines starting with <<<<<<<, =======, and >>>>>>>. Keep the code you want and delete the markers. Then git add the file and git commit to finish the merge.
learn.code:
<<<<<<< HEAD
color = 'red'
=======
color = 'blue'
>>>>>>> login

# keep one, remove markers

qs.why: Merge the other branch into the one you are on.

qs.why: Git cannot choose between competing edits.

qs.q: In this file, what is the part between the ======= line and the >>>>>>> line?
qs.why: The top is HEAD, the bottom is the merged branch.

qs.q: After fixing the conflict markers you must git add the file and commit.
qs.why: That finishes the merge.

qs.q: Match each term to its meaning
pairs: Same lines changed in both branches

learn.b: A remote is a copy of your repository stored somewhere else, usually on GitHub. By convention the main remote is named origin. git remote -v lists remotes with their URLs.
learn.code:
git remote add origin https://github.com/ana/game.git
git remote -v

learn.b: git push sends your local commits to the remote. The first time on a new branch use -u so Git remembers the link, like git push -u origin main. After that, plain git push is enough.
learn.code:
git push -u origin main
git push

learn.b: git pull downloads new commits from the remote and merges them into your branch. git fetch only downloads them and leaves your files alone, so you can look first. Pull equals fetch plus merge.
git clone URL copies an entire repository, with all its history, onto your computer. It also sets origin for you. Use it once to get a project, and then use pull to stay updated.
learn.code: git clone https://github.com/ana/game.git

learn.b: A pull request, or PR, is a request to merge your branch into another one, usually main. You push your branch to GitHub and open a PR on the website. Teammates can read your changes and discuss them before anything is merged.
Create a branch, commit your work, push the branch, then open the PR. GitHub shows the changed lines, called the diff. Give the PR a clear title and describe what and why.

Reviewers comment on specific lines and then approve, comment, or request changes. If changes are requested, you commit more fixes to the same branch and the PR updates by itself. Reviews catch bugs and share knowledge.
learn.code:
git switch -c fix-typo
git commit -m "Fix typo"
git push -u origin fix-typo

learn.b: When the PR is approved and checks pass, someone clicks Merge. GitHub offers merge commit, squash (all commits become one), or rebase. After merging you can delete the branch and pull main locally. Forking copies someone else's repo to your account so you can open PRs to it.

qs.q: What is a pull request?

qs.why: PRs ask for review and merge.

qs.q: A reviewer asks for changes. What do you do?

qs.why: The PR updates when you push to its branch.

qs.q: Which step comes right before opening a PR on GitHub?

qs.why: GitHub needs your branch on the remote.

qs.why: Squash gives a tidy single commit.

learn.b: git restore file throws away your unsaved changes in that file and brings back the last committed version. This cannot be undone, so be sure. To unstage a file without losing edits use git restore --staged file.
learn.code:
git restore app.js
git restore --staged app.js

learn.b: git revert ID makes a new commit that does the opposite of an old commit. History is kept, so it is safe even for commits you already pushed. Use it on shared branches.
learn.code: git revert a1b2c3d

learn.b: git reset moves your branch pointer to an older commit. With --soft the changes stay staged, with the default mixed they stay in your files, and with --hard they are deleted. Resetting rewrites history, so avoid it on commits others already have.
learn.code:
git reset --soft HEAD~1
git reset --hard HEAD~1

learn.b: If you only mistyped the last message or forgot a file, use git commit --amend. It replaces the last commit with a new one. Only amend commits you have not pushed. HEAD~1 means one commit before HEAD.
learn.code:
git add forgot.txt
git commit --amend -m "Better message"

qs.why: Revert adds a new commit without rewriting history.

learn.b: Most teams use feature branches: main always works, and every new feature or fix gets its own short branch and a PR. Name branches clearly, like feature/login or fix/typo. Commit small and often, and pull before you push.

A tag is a permanent label on a commit, often used for releases like v1.0. Create a lightweight tag with git tag v1.0 and an annotated one with git tag -a v1.0 -m "First release". Tags are not pushed automatically, so push them yourself.
learn.code:
git tag -a v1.0 -m "First release"
git push origin v1.0

learn.b: GitHub Actions runs commands for you automatically when something happens, such as a push. It is used to run tests, build projects and deploy. You describe it in a YAML file inside .github/workflows.
A workflow lists when it runs (on), and jobs made of steps. This one runs your tests on every push. If a step fails, the commit gets a red mark on GitHub, which tells you something broke.
learn.code:
name: Tests
on: push
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test

qs.q: What is a tag in Git?
o: A kind of branch that moves
A permanent label on a commit
qs.why: Tags mark releases like v1.0.
